title: Sulawesi
wiki_lead:
Sulawesi ( SOO-lə-WAY-see, Indonesian: [ˌsulaˈwesi]; Lontara: ᨔᨘᨒᨓᨙᨔᨗ romanized: Sulawési), also known as Celebes, is an island in Indonesia. One of the four Greater Sunda Islands, and the world's 11th-largest island, it is situated east of Borneo, west of the Maluku Islands, and south of Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago. Within Indonesia, only Sumatra, Borneo, and Papua are larger in territory, and only Java and Sumatra are more populous.
The landmass of Sulawesi includes four peninsulas: the northern Minahasa Peninsula, the East Peninsula, the South Peninsula, and the Southeast Peninsula. Three gulfs separate these peninsulas: the Gulf of Tomini between the northern Minahasa and East peninsulas, the Gulf of Tolo between the East and Southeast peninsulas, and the Gulf of Boni between the South and Southeast peninsulas. The Makassar Strait runs along the western side of the island and separates the island from Borneo.
wiki_excerpt:
Sulawesi ( SOO-lə-WAY-see, Indonesian: [ˌsulaˈwesi]; Lontara: ᨔᨘᨒᨓᨙᨔᨗ romanized: Sulawési), also known as Celebes, is an island in Indonesia. One of the four Greater Sunda Islands, and the world's 11th-largest island, it is situated east of Borneo, west of the Maluku Islands, and south of Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago. Within Indonesia, only Sumatra, Borneo, and Papua are larger in territory, and only Java and Sumatra are more populous.
The landmass of Sulawesi includes four peninsulas: the northern Minahasa Peninsula, the East Peninsula, the South Peninsula, and the Southeast Peninsula. Three gulfs separate these peninsulas: the Gulf of Tomini between the northern Minahasa and East peninsulas, the Gulf of Tolo between the East and Southeast peninsulas, and the Gulf of Boni between the South and Southeast peninsulas. The Makassar Strait runs along the western side of the island and separates the island from Borneo.


Etymology
The name Celebes ( SEL-ib-eez, sə-LEE-beez) was originally given to the island by Portuguese explorers. First recorded in 1512, it may come from Os Célebres, 'the famous ones', referring to some prominent rocks; the interrelationship between the Portuguese name and the local name Sulawesi is uncertain. Tomé Pires called the northeast tip of the island Punta de Celebres (point of currents) in 1515. From the 17th century, the Dutch were referring to the island as Selebessi.
The second element may come from the Proto-Malayo-Chamic root *bəsi, "iron," but the origin of the first is uncertain. The first part is sometimes derived from Sanskrit शूल॑ (śū́la, 'dagger, stake'), referring to the sharp peninsulas, jagged mountains and treacherous offshore rocks.


Geography
Sulawesi is the world's eleventh-largest island, covering an area of 186,064.34 km2 (71,840 sq mi) (including minor islands administered as part of Sulawesi). The central part of the island is ruggedly mountainous, such that the island's peninsulas have traditionally been remote from each other, with better connections by sea than by road. The three bays that divide Sulawesi's peninsulas are, from north to south, the Tomini, the Tolo and the Boni. These separate the Minahasa or Northern Peninsula, the East Peninsula, the Southeast Peninsula and the South Peninsula.
The Strait of Makassar runs along the western side of the island. The island is surrounded by Borneo to the west, by the Philippines to the north, by Maluku to the east, and by Flores and Timor to the south.


Minor islands
The Selayar Islands make up a chain stretching southwards from Southwest Sulawesi into the Flores Sea are administratively part of Sulawesi. The Sangihe Islands and Talaud Islands stretch northward from the northeastern tip of Sulawesi, while Buton and Muna Islands and their neighbors lie off its southeast peninsula, the Togian Islands are in the Gulf of Tomini, and Peleng Island and the Banggai Islands form a cluster between Sulawesi and Maluku. All the above-mentioned islands and many smaller ones off the coasts of Sulawesi are administratively part of Sulawesi's six provinces.


Geology

The island slopes up from the shores of the deep seas surrounding the island to a high and mostly non-volcanic, mountainous interior. Active volcanoes are found in the northern Minahasa Peninsula, stretching north to the Sangihe Islands. The northern peninsula contains several active volcanoes such as Mount Lokon, Mount Awu, Soputan and Karangetang.
According to plate reconstructions, the island is believed to have been formed by the collision of terranes from the Asian Plate (forming the west and southwest) and from the Australian Plate (forming the southeast and Banggai), with island arcs previously in the Pacific (forming the north and east peninsulas). Because of its several tectonic origins, various faults scar the land and as a result the island is prone to earthquakes, including the deadly 2018 and 2021 quakes.

grok_lead: Sulawesi is a large, irregularly shaped island in Indonesia, situated in the Wallacea biogeographic region between Borneo and the Maluku Islands, with an area of 174,600 square kilometers that ranks it as the world's eleventh-largest island. The island's distinctive K-like outline results from its mountainous interior, volcanic activity, and peninsular extensions, encompassing diverse ecosystems from rainforests to coral reefs. As of recent estimates, its population exceeds 20 million, concentrated in coastal cities like Makassar, the largest urban center. Sulawesi's position in Wallacea has fostered exceptional biodiversity, with high rates of endemism driven by historical isolation and varied habitats; it hosts over 350 bird species, including 96 endemics like the maleo megapode, and numerous unique mammals such as seven species of macaques and the anoa dwarf buffalo. Vascular plant diversity includes nearly 6,000 species, over a third of which are endemic, supporting complex food webs and evolutionary radiations. These biological riches, however, face pressures from deforestation, mining, and agricultural expansion, underscoring causal links between human activity and habitat loss. The island's human history reflects Austronesian migrations and indigenous adaptations, yielding diverse ethnic groups including the seafaring Bugis and Makassarese in the south, highland Toraja with their megalithic burial practices, and northern Minahasa communities influenced by trade and missionary activity. Prehistoric evidence, such as cave art and tools dating back tens of thousands of years, indicates early human presence amid Wallacean faunal assemblages. These cultures have sustained animist traditions alongside predominant Islam in the south and Christianity in the north, shaping social structures resilient to colonial and modern influences.
